articles.text: The following letter was sent to Piedmont School District and Piedmont School Board. Last March, our school board, the Superintendent, and Alameda County acted on the best available information at the time and closed our schools to help stop the spread of the COVID-19 virus. With limited data about the virus, this decision seemed wise and one that we, as medical professionals, supported at the time. In the intervening 10 months, we have learned a lot about the biology and epidemiology of the virus, both how it is transmitted and how to treat it. Early on, we assumed that children would be primary drivers of the virus. This assumption was later disproved. During these months, we have also watched as schools elsewhere found ways to reopen safely. Our initial reaction was one of caution and concern, wondering if this was the right decision. Then, data from school reopenings began to surface and it became apparent that with the appropriate safety measures in place, schools could in fact safely provide in-person instruction. It also became very apparent that the longer we kept our students out of the classroom, and the longer they were subject to distance-learning, the more harm we were doing to them. Without a doubt distance-learning is causing tremendous learning loss and profound mental health crises in children across all age spectrums. Data shows a significant increase in the number of children disclosing suicidal ideation, and dealing with acute mental health crises and eating disorders stemming from depression, anxiety, and social isolation. It is now clear that ongoing school closures are not based on evidence. Yet, despite all of this information, and despite the very serious calls from parents, students, scientists, and medical experts to reopen our schools, children in Piedmont remain in full-time distance-learning. It is abundantly clear that the decisions made by the Alameda County Public Health Department, by PUSD’s administration, and the school board have not served the best interest of our children. There should be no more delay. There should be no more excuses. It’s time to open our schools. It’s time to honor the science we teach our students. As medical and mental health professionals, we implore PUSD to return to in-person education for all students. With millions of school children around the world safely back in the classroom with their peers and teachers, we know that it can be done. articles.text: An optimistic plan has been set for Piedmont elementary schools to start a phased reopening on Tuesday, February 9. All students in grades TK-5 should be back in classrooms by February 25, according to School Superintendent Randy Booker. An e-mail message sent January 25 to parents of Piedmont provided details of a plan he will be presenting to the Piedmont School Board at its meeting tonight, January 27. “This phased-in plan assumes that beginning on Feb. 1st case rates [in Alameda County] have dropped below 25 per 100,000. If it hasn’t, we will have to push back our timeline accordingly,” his message read. Governor Newsom’s Safe Schools for All Plan (at schools. covid19.ca.gov) permits elementary students to return to campus when county-level Covid infection rates drop below an adjusted value of 25 new cases per day per 100,000 for five consecutive days. Case numbers include a seven-day lag and are a seven-day average, meaning the rate is determined by data from 7-14 days prior. Newsom’s plan marks an easing of the previous restriction which required case numbers to be under seven per day, per 100,000. articles.text: On contemporary banking, redefining the term incompetence As you know, Wiley has had his share of issues with Big Banks in the past. Back in June of 2016, he even conned the Editor of the Post to publish one of his horror stories, which still gives him bad dreams at night. (For background, see http://wholehoag.blogspot.com/) Well, it must run in the family, because Mrs. Wiley, aka The LW, had her own surreal experience with another Big Bank this week. And it was even worse than Wiley’s, because it involved Real People, and because we don’t even bank with them. Before we go any further, you have to understand that The LW is smarter than Wiley (not too hard, she would say), and that she had been a senior executive with a Big Bank Predecessor in a prior life. In fact, had she not decided to work part time for a few years to spend more time raising the kids, she probably would have risen to the top of their Good Old Boy Team. And, unlike Wiley, she knows how to deal with people, so when she has a people problem, you know it’s a bona fide People Problem. At any rate, The LW got a letter the other day from said Bank. When she opened it, she saw that it was addressed to her AND four other people. Now, unless she has been hiding something really serious, these people do not live at our address, and have not at any time in the 37 years we’ve been here. And that is a good thing, because two of them died a number of years ago, and if they really lived with us, LW would definitely have some explaining to do. articles.text: State announces plan to prioritize age in vaccine rollout California announced changes to its complex COVID-19 vaccine distribution plan yesterday, Tuesday, January 26. Now, people 65 years of age and older, as well as workers in education, childcare, food, grocery and agriculture sectors, are eligible to receive the vaccine statewide. This group amounts to about 8.5 million Californians. This group is in addition to the initial group that began receiving the vaccine in December, which is comprised of healthcare workers as well as the residents and staff of long-term care facilities. This group of people, numbering an estimated 3 million statewide, are still receiving vaccines. Beyond these groups, California will prioritize vaccine administration based on age, a significant change from earlier plans. The details of who will receive the vaccine next is still being hammered out by the state, but this next phase is expected to begin sometime in the spring. this year, anyone who wants to receive a COVID-19 vaccine should be able to receive it, the state believes. With vaccine supply and the state’s distribution plans in flux, the timetable is subject to change. California’s Health and Human Services Secretary Mark Ghaly said at a press conference yesterday, January 26, that the state is now vaccinating 125,000 people every weekday, a huge increase in distribution since last month. The state is encouraging residents to utilize a new digital “My Turn” notification tool at myturn. ca.gov. On the website, Californians can find out their eligibility and, if eligible, they can schedule a vaccination appointment. Those who are not eligible for vaccination can sign up for notifications when it is their turn. While some hospitals and counties were vaccinating senior citizens earlier this month, everyone age 65 and older are now eligible statewide. The state has administered almost 2.6 million vaccine doses out of a stockpile of about 4.6 million doses, according to the California Department of Public Health. Importantly, both the Pfizer and Moderna vaccine that are being used in California require patients to receive two doses of vaccine administered several weeks apart. As of press time, over 371,000 people have received their second dose in California. California is still amongst the worst states in terms of vaccine distribution so far, even though it holds more total doses than any other state. As of Monday, January 25, Alameda County possesses 102,750 doses of the vaccine. Roughly half of these doses were manufactured by Pfizer and the other half were created by Moderna. Almost 64,000 of these doses have been passed onto healthcare facilities, while about 39,000 are being administered by the Alameda County Public Health Department. Of the latter, the ACPHD has already administered 54 percent of these doses as of last week. Demand continues to outstrip vaccine supply. Phase 1A, the group of healthcare workers and residents of long-term care facilities that were first eligible for vaccination, is estimated to number more than 145,000 people in Alameda County. Along with using the My Tool website, the county encourages people 65 years and older to contact their healthcare provider to see if vaccine doses are available now.
articles.title: Age 65 and older now eligible for COVID-19 vaccine

articles.text: Szczech presents midyear report to City Council A midyear fiscal report for fiscal year 2020–2021 was presented by Piedmont Finance Director Michael Szczech to the city council at its January 19 meeting. The report found that the city’s general fund remains in a sound position, with revenues exceeding expenses. Szczech contributed this to “conservative budgeting, a strong real estate market [even with Covid], and prudent management of day-today operations.” The city’s finance department projects general fund revenues to exceed budget by approximately $2.4 million, and expenses to be lower than budget by approximately $400,000. Increase in revenue is largely from “higher than expected real property transfer tax receipts,” as well as mutual aid revenue for wildfire assistance, increased building permits, property tax receipts, and other taxes. pages.text: Wednesday, January 27, 2021 3 News Age 65 and older now eligible for COVID-19 vaccine State announces plan to prioritize age in vaccine rollout By Barry Eitel California announced changes to its complex COVID-19 vaccine distribution plan yesterday, Tuesday, January 26. Now, people 65 years of age and older, as well as workers in education, childcare, food, grocery and agriculture sectors, are eligible to receive the vaccine statewide. This group amounts to about 8.5 million Californians. This group is in addition to the initial group that began receiving the vaccine in December, which is comprised of healthcare workers as well as the residents and staff of long-term care facilities. This group of people, numbering an estimated 3 million statewide, are still receiving vaccines. Beyond these groups, California will prioritize vaccine administration based on age, a significant change from earlier plans. The details of who will receive the vaccine next is still being hammered out by the state, but this next phase is expected to begin sometime in the spring. By the summer and fall of this year, anyone who wants to receive a COVID-19 vaccine should be able to receive it, the state believes. With vaccine supply and the state’s distribution plans in flux, the timetable is subject to change. California’s Health and Human Services Secretary Mark Ghaly said at a press conference yesterday, January 26, that the state is now vaccinating 125,000 people every weekday, a huge increase in distribution since last month. The state is encouraging residents to utilize a new digital “My Turn” notification tool at myturn. ca.gov. On the website, Californians can find out their eligibility and, if eligible, they can schedule a vaccination appointment. Those who are not eligible for vaccination can sign up for notifications when it is their turn. While some hospitals and counties were vaccinating senior citizens earlier this month, everyone age 65 and older are now eligible statewide. The state has administered almost 2.6 million vaccine doses out of a stockpile of about 4.6 million doses, according to the California Department of Public Health. Importantly, both the Pfizer and Moderna vaccine that are being used in California require patients to receive two doses of vaccine administered several weeks apart. articles.text: Editor: Last week, the Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee (PADC), formerly the Piedmont Appreciating Diversity Committee, hosted the 24th annual Martin Luther King Jr. Day Celebration in partnership with the City of Piedmont. The theme was “Let Us Be Dissatisfied: Using Our Power to Bend the Arc,” recognizing that the power to fix the problems Dr. King called out over 50 years ago is in our hands. Speakers included Stanford University Professor Clayborne Carson, Congresswoman Barbara Lee, Senator Nancy Skinner and Piedmont Councilmember Tim Rood. Here in Piedmont, the willingness to address racial reckoning gave rise to racial justice resolutions passed by City Council and the School Board; a month-long flag display in support of Black Lives Matter; PUSD’s new equity policies; and a website created by resident Meghan Bennett detailing the shameful treatment and ouster of Piedmont’s first black homeowner. While working with city and school district officials on racial equity resolutions and policies, PADC took a moment to reflect on our own decades of work and envision what was next. We changed our name from “Appreciating Diversity” to “Anti-Racism and Diversity.” Our renewed mission is dedicated to rooting out racism and embracing diversity and inclusion. Our values are inclusive community, racial equity, learning culture, collective action, and transparency. We award grants to educators and community members working to advance inclusion and racial equity. Amid a global pandemic, we moved this year’s MLK event to a virtual platform. We invited partners to develop workshops. One of those, co-created by PADC and PREC, is the Jan. 28 panel discussion “Reimagining Public Safety: Can Surveillance be a Fair and Effective Tool?” PADC designed this year’s King program to provide us with tools to confront our own blind spots and move towards greater understanding and connection. We are committed to creating a more inclusive Piedmont. The MLK celebration is not just a call to honor a memory. It is a continuation of King’s work to raise our consciousness and lift up our community into the light of a new day. To do so means we must all step out of our comfort zones and build a new and better world. –Sheila Leunig and Jennifer Long PADC Co-presidents Request a Virtual or On-Site Quote

articles.text: The Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee (PADC) and the Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign (PREC) will host a virtual panel at 7 p.m. tomorrow, January 28, entitled “Reimagining Public Safety: Can Surveillance Be a Fair and Effective Tool?” The panel is also co-sponsored by the League of Women Voters of Piedmont. The panel discussion will include key individuals in the public safety sector and is a follow-up to a similar panel that the League of Woman Voters held in 2017. Piedmont’s Police Chief Jeremy Bowers will participate, along with Brian Hofer (Chair of the Oakland Privacy Advisory Commission), Jennifer Jones (Technology and Civil Liberties Fellow, ACLU Northern California) and Mathew Guariglia (Policy Analyst for Electronic Frontier Foundation). The virtual discussion, available via teleconference application Zoom, focuses on how surveillance impacts racial justice and public safety in Piedmont and the broader community. New surveillance technologies monitor, track, and predict the actions of citizens, and are becoming increasingly popular in public safety. The discussion explores whether these new technologies can usher in a new era of unbiased, inexpensive public safety and justice or if they are inherently problematic. Featured speakers will delve in to whether or not they can be used fairly and effectively within the context of our flawed public safety and justice system. The Zoom panel discussion will begin at 7 p.m., and is expected to end at 8:30 p.m. To register for the event, visit: https:// www.lwvpiedmont.org/content. a spx?page_id= 40 02&club_ id=601389&item_id=1363151

articles.text: The Piedmont City Council will have a second reading of the proposed energy reach codes at its February 1 meeting. Potential energy reach codes were considered by city council during a first reading in July 2020. The first reading was approved, but councilmembers directed staff to complete additional public outreach and education before the second reading. On September 3, 2020, the city hosted a virtual town hall meeting via Zoom to provide an opportunity for residents to ask questions and learn more about the proposal. In November and December last year the research firm FM3 conducted an additional survey to complement a survey that was completed earlier in the year. Dave Metz, President of FM3, presented the results of that survey to city council on January 19. The January 19 meeting provided an informational update on public engagement related to reach codes, and adoption of reach codes was not considered at the meeting. The key takeaways from that survey found that residents’ view of reach codes as proposed is positive. The results stated that 64 percent of respondents supported requiring these improvements in order to reduce natural gas. The survey was administrated to a random representative sample of Piedmont’s registered voters, so results suggest that a majority of residents support both the overall idea of revising building codes and the specific code amendments included in the ordinances. Staff will bring forward the second reading at the next city council meeting. The report at that meeting will address lingering concerns and will include additional clarification about requirements and exemptions, according to Planning Department staff.

articles.text: A parent called me recently, convinced that her son needed to go to a different school, maybe one that does one-on-one tutoring, or perhaps a wilderness program. While there’s nothing wrong with either choice, changing schools in the middle of a school year is a dramatic move. I generally advise parents to make sure the solution matches the problem. What’s going on? I asked, hoping to help her make sense of the situation. I’m convinced my son isn’t learning anything, she explained. I think he plays video games all day long, and I don’t think he’s very engaged in what’s happening in his Zoom classes. articles.text: Nominations for Piedmont School District’s annual Art Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award are now being accepted. The deadline for nominations is March 15, 2021. A selection committee will vote on the award recipient, who will be recognized at the May 12 Board of Education meeting. The honoree also will receive the gift of a work of student art. The student will receive a monetary award and commendation from the Board. The award is presented annually to individuals who have volunteered their efforts over a period of time and made a difference because of their involvement and commitment to Piedmont’s youth. The first winner in 1998 was Hunter McCreary, founder of PLOT (Piedmont Light Opera Theatre). Last year’s winner was Sue Smegal, a former teacher, school board member, and longtime active supporter of Piedmont schools. Art Hecht, a former school board member, was a tireless community volunteer dedicated to students in both Piedmont and Oakland. He served on Piedmont’s Board of Education from 1970 to 1978 and was a champion of Piedmont Continuation High School, the forerunner of Millennium High. The Art Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award was established by former school board president Dewey Watson in 1998 to honor the legacy of Mr. Hecht. The deadline for nominations is March 16, 2020. A selection committee will vote on the award recipient, who will be recognized at the May 12, School Board meeting. Nomination forms are available on the PUSD website and in the school district office, 760 Magnolia Avenue.

Over 700 people joined the online event. Other Garden Clubs participating included Orinda, Marin, Hillsborough, Woodside-Atherton, and Carmel-by-the-Sea. The symposium was introduced by Julia Burke, a member of the Piedmont Garden Club and Bay Visions Committee. The Bay Visions Committee is formed by the six chapters of The Garden Club of America (GCA) with a mission to protect and restore the region’s defining bays and estuaries. The Committee works to educate its members and their communities on the bay’s critical importance to the environment. The latest virtual event, “Bay Visions 2021: The Power of Plants will Protect the Bay,” was a two-hour look at adaption, regeneration, and the role plants play in mitigating the challenges facing the San Francisco Bay. “Our goal [with the symposium] is to inspire others to be as excited as we are about the successful work being done to protect and restore the Bay utilizing plants underwater, in wetlands, along the shoreline, and upland,” explained Lori Adams, President of the Piedmont Garden Club. The program began with a slide show that featured CGA Northern California Partners for Plants (P4P) restoration projects. Each club’s efforts for Bay restoration are supported and encouraged by the Bay Visions Committee. Featured restoration projects included Carmel-by-theSea Garden Club’s North Dunes restoration, Hillsborough Garden Club’s Heron’s Head Park project, and Piedmont and Orinda Garden Clubs’ combined MLK Shoreline project. Their shoreline volunteer restoration project was at Oakport Park at Martin Luther King, Jr. Shoreline across the freeway from the Oakland Coliseum, an area that was originally wetlands. The two garden clubs worked to remove invasive plants and grasses and spread organic soil for fill. But Biden’s attention was first focused on averting U.S. domestic disasters as he hit the ground running last Wednesday on Inaugural Day, January 20. Addressing his most urgent priorities, Biden halted the nation’s withdrawal from the World Health Organization; rejoined the Paris Climate Accord; canceled the Keystone XL pipeline; ordered mask-wearing on federal property for 100 days; ordered FEMA to open vaccination centers and OSHA to enforce worker safety; straightened out coronavirus data collection; set in motion new preventive measures against pandemic threats; ordered new guidelines for schools to open; reset international travel restrictions; lifted the ban on travel by people from Muslim countries; strengthened Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals or DACA rules; halted the construction of the wall between the U.S. and Mexico; and paused the repayment of student loans until at least September 30. Altogether, he signed about 30 executive orders in his first three days on the job. Biden spoke to North American leaders, Canada’s Prime Minister Justin Trudeau and Mexico’s President Andrés Manuel López Obrador, and then spoke to the United Kingdom’s PM Boris Johnson, who is eager to drive a virtual G7 summit in a matter of weeks. He is ambitiously targeting climate threats, Covid-19, future pandemic preparedness, and relations with China. The U.K. leader is this year’s G7 summit president, a rotating title, and as the country’s host for the coming face-to-face June event, he is plowing ahead changing the G7 into a D-10. Such is his prerogative to set the agenda. According to The Guardian, “U.S. thinktanks have pushed” for the Group of 7 nations (France, U.K., Italy, Canada, Germany, Japan, and U.S.) to expand into a democracies of the world group to include India, South Korea, and Australia.” The change is not without consternation from European nations, and in particular, France and Italy are concerned about diluting their G7 power and the appearance of an anti-China maneuver. The Russian Federation joined in 1998, though Russia never ranked as a major advanced economy by International Monetary Fund indices; but when Russia forcibly annexed Crimea (from Ukraine) in March 2014, the body politic suspended Russia, and the G8 reverted to G7 again. Former president Donald Trump was G7 president for the 2020 summit that was canceled due to Covid-19. At the time he Britain’s Prime Minister Boris Johnson spoke to President Biden about deepening the long-standing alliance between the two countries; support for NATO; and the potential for a free-trade deal. President Joe Biden warns of surpassing 600,000 U.S. deaths and the need to move fast on passing his $1.9 trillion Rescue plan against Covid-19. Post WWII England was one of the “Inner Six” organized for economic prosperity by the Treaty of Paris, which bloomed into the European Economic Community, and then the European Union in the 1960s. England joined in 1973, but the first referendum was three year later when 67 percent voted to stay. England’s 2016 referendum capped years of interior conflicts -- contentious issues that were amplified by geo-political, economic, cultural, and demographic divisions. While London elites enjoyed economic prosperity and voted to Remain, North county laborers struggled in dying industries and voted to roll the dice and Leave. “Eurosceptics,” generally older conservatives who steadfastly criticized E.U. governance and lamented U.K.’s loss of sovereignty, they voted to Leave and rid themselves of the heavy taxpayer burden, forced immigrant quotas, and regulations imposing on their freedoms. One commonplace notion is that England was always an “awkward” E.U. partner; and different than the continent, because she’s an island nation and recognized as a global power. Brits use the The temperature sank to 27º with a dusting of snow in Paris that rarely lasts more than a day: a courtyard view (left) from my window and (right) from a friend’s window facing Château de Vincennes. lobbied publicly for Russia to rejoin, an unpopular premise lacking merit. He did however voice support for South Korea, Australia, and India. PM Boris Johnson is anxious to establish trade deals with allies, now that Britain’s trade with the European Union is much curtailed by new agreements finalized just days prior to the January 1st launch of U.K.’s new sovereignty. Brexit is shorthand for “British exit,” and the exit is complete, but the result is that England is besieged by traffic jams at the ports and a wild confusion of processes not yet set in place. The origin of Brexit began in 2013 when Conservative Party leader David Cameron pledged a national referendum on E.U. membership to finally settle the question once and for all. Voters were presented in 2016 with the broad question of whether the U.K. should leave or remain in the European Union. Cameron was certain the vote would be to remain, but by a slim margin of 51.8% the Brits chose to leave. U.K.’s vast array of trade, security, and migration agreements entwined with the continent had matured greatly during 47 years of association, and the ties have proved extraordinarily complex to disentangle. Brexit traffic jam of 17 miles due to new required paperwork for custom duties due to the U.K. no longer being in the European Union bloc. Blame it on Brexit: Lorries idle in both directions due to new required custom invoices now that U.K. is no longer an E.U. member.

pages.text: 12 Wednesday, January 27, 2021 HIKING WITH JON Donner Pass – a mystifying, stimulating winter adventure By Jonathan Comeaux This treasure of California is among the best wintertime hikes in the Sierra Nevada. Donner Pass, an abandoned railway that was originally constructed in 1867 for the Central Pacific Railroad’s portion of the First Transcontinental Railroad. The trek takes you through hollowed out mountain tunnels and snow sheds through the pass above Donner Lake. Staff Photos The starting point for the trail from McGlashan Point, up a popular sledding hill to China Wall and the first tunnel. China Wall is a platform created by Chinese workers to create the Central Pacific Railroad in 1868. Snow piles into some sections of the Donner Pass trail. Free Delivery to Piedmont Open Wednesday to Sunday • 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. A view of Donner Lake and the Donner Pass snow sheds appropriately covered in snow. Aside from the obvious historic railway, the mountain pass is the same area where the Donner Party tragically met their fate in the fierce winter of 1846—becoming the namesake of the lake and surrounding state park. The walk through the train tunnels is brief at just 2.1 miles to the final snow shed, but it gives you the magic of the Tahoe winter without being knee deep in snow. It’s a great place for children, families, or beginning snowshoers. During the warmer weather, you can walk past the last snow shed and continue to Donner Peak. From our starting point, we took the same route as our 2018 summer visit from McGlashan Point over a Native American petroglyph site that can be seen in warmer months. For now, it’s a popular sledding site with fresh snow. The Central Pacific Railroad created its route through Donner Pass in the spring of 1868 after a near three-year construction effort, accomplished through the efforts of Chinese railroad workers. The Donner Pass trail’s starting point, the China Wall, is a handmade construction that was the platform for the railroad leading into the starting tunnel. Inside the 1,659 foot Tunnel #6, hikers can spot a second Chinese Wall with boulders piled neatly up to the roof. Through the hollowed out mountains, some large icicles glisten through the tiny peaks of light along the roof and walls. Even some large frozen sections of water created massive blocks of ice that are clear as a piece of glass. You’ll find few sites that combine history and artwork with graffiti covering each wall of the sheds — some pieces magnificent in detail. Peeking around unsuspecting corners and behind walls, walkers with keen eyes can find some of California’s most prominent urban artists and large murals. Proper hiking gear is required in some ice-covered areas to prevent slipping and falls. With limited parking at the entrance lot to the tunnels, some may have to park n the sside of Donner Pass Road or at the Donner Lake Overlook. In our five miles of hiking, we passed just 27 hikers. Another 13 were huddled around the starting area’s sledding hill toward the A frozen wall of ice creates a surreal sigh inside a snowshed. The tunnel opens and begins a walk through some fresh powder. Above is a view of Donner Peak. China Wall. To access this area, hikers can punch in Donner Pass, Summit Haus, or Donner Lake Overlook on their GPS devices for common starting areas. Remember to return in the summer to see petroglyphs along McGlashan Point and fr a hike to Donner Peak. A long tunnel through the mountains is part of a second China Wall above Lake Donner. The entire walk has graffiti-covered walls inside the snow sheds. Some are distinctly graffiti art, such as the one on the right.

articles.text: The Golden State Warriors recently submitted an extensive plan to state and local officials to host 9,000 fans each game, representing 50 percent of the stadium’s capacity. The proposal, which relies on rapid PCR testing of everyone entering the building, was rejected by San Francisco health officials before the season last November. On November 18, a date prior to large spikes in the number of COVID cases reported and prior to the announcement of a vaccine becoming available, San Francisco health officer Tomás Aragón said the city may be willing to work with the team on a plan for a 25 percent capacity crowd, once San Francisco reaches the state’s yellow tier of reopening. Seven NBA teams currently allow limited fan capacity in their arenas. Tomorrow, January 28, the Miami Heat will start allowing 10 percent capacity in their arena with the help of coronavirus sniffing dogs. Before you say “only in Miami,” coronavirus-sniffing dogs have been put to work in airports of Dubai and Helsinki in recent months. The Warriors consulted with Dr. George Rutherford, a Professor of Epidemiology at UCSF. All fans, players, staff, and everyone entering Chase Center would have to pass a PCR-polymerase chain reaction rapid test on game day or with 48 hours prior to the game. PCR testing looks for the RNA of the virus itself and has a sensitivity rating of at least 97 percent efficient. In an interview with the Post, Dr. Rutherford called PCR testing “State of the art. It is way sophisticated – and also way expensive, too.” In comparison, antigen tests look for proteins shed from the surface of the virus. The virus’ RNA has to already be incorporated and making viruses in order to show up on an antigen test, making the accuracy much lower. Warriors owner Joe Lacob said he was willing to spend upward of $30 million dollars for testing this year. Lacob has a master’s degree in public health from UCLA and is a venture capitalist in biotechnology. Temperature and symptoms screening would weed out a portion of false negatives from the PCR tests. Rutherford noted “It provides this really high, high, level of assurance that people walking through the door aren’t going to be infectious.” Further curtailing of possible transmission would result from mask wearing, physical distancing and the usage of a ventilation system capable of replacing all the air in the arena every 15 minutes. Attendees would mostly be season ticket holders that get tested beforehand to have results within 48 hours. Rutherford said there was not a concern about contracting and spreading the virus during the 48-hour gap. “It takes basically four days from the time you are exposed to the time you become infectious. [Contracting and spreading] could theoretically happen, but I don’t think so,” he said. While Rutherford liked the details of the plan, everything depends upon community infection levels. “[The case numbers] are too high right now [January 10]. It is just a very uncomfortable position. This is serious stuff and the reason everyone is being inconvenienced is because it is serious stuff,” he said. After a number of championship years, the Warriors finished last in the league last year. With the return of Steph Curry and by adding the second pick in the draft, 19-year-old 7-footer James Wiseman, the Warriors are rebuilding an exciting and competitive team. High COVID case counts, slow vaccine roll out and San Francisco’s track record of enforcing pre-emptive and stringent COVID restrictions make the prospects of attending a game look bleak. Short of a miraculous turnaround or an unexpected great development, like foolproof Covid-sniffing dogs, it looks like the only way to see the team this year will be through a screen – or traveling out of state to see them play any of the seven teams playing live before audiences.

articles.text: Tom Brady, the Serra High School grad and 43-year old NFL living legend, has taken the Buccaneers to Super Bowl after upsetting the top-seeded Green Bay Packers 31-26 to face the defending champion Chiefs. But then again, can we really say that we’re surprised Brady is back? The 55th Super Bowl will take place on February 7 in Tampa Bay, Florida, becoming the first hosting team to also play in the game. Regardless of the outcome, which team you’re rooting for, or whether you love or despise Brady or Patrick Mahomes; take a second to appreciate these two wondrous quarterbacks. In Brady’s 21 years, he has reached the NFL’s postseason 18 times, building a 33-11 playoff record including 10 Super Bowl appearances. He’s undoubtedly the game’s best ever. Mahomes is a superstar every bit deserving of his 10-year, $450 million contract and only four years into his career. The 25-year old is a wizard with the football, delivering passes at odd angles. He’s considered perhaps the most dynamic player at his position, and that includes Brady. The Chiefs are a slight favorite, and this writer has a hard time counting out KC’s dynamic roster. But how could you not see Brady pulling off his Super Bowl magic? Sit back, watch, and enjoy. 49ers Notes The San Francisco quarterback controversy has begun with the 49ers reportedly having some interest in trading for Lions QB Matthew Stafford. However, this writer isn’t buying it. All indications have been that Jimmy Garoppolo is still in good standing with coach Kyle Shanahan, while the cost to acquire Stafford would likely be multiple picks included with a firstrounder. That doesn’t seem likely with the 49ers only having one second-round selection. Raiders Notes As for QB Derek Carr, you can never say never with Jon Gruden calling the shots for the Vegas Raiders. Maybe a blockbuster deal for Texans’ QB Deshaun Watson? articles.text: The English Premier League is at its midway point of its 38-game soccer season. Seven teams are within nine points of the top spot, Manchester City (12-5-2, 41 points). But the major news coming out of England has been the firing of Chelsea manager Frank Lampard on January 25. His team is sitting far down the table in 10th at 8-5-6 with just 29 points. The team hired Thomas Tuchel, the former Paris St. Germain manager, to take over for the remainder of the season. The pressure to succeed at Chelsea is quite impossible. Lampard’s 14-year playing career with the Blues wasn’t enough to convince patience from ownership after just one full season at the helm. But the news coming out of London about Lampard was condemning. The Athletic reported that veteran center back Antonio Rudiger and midfielder Mateo Kovačić went to the front office claiming that Lampard was “quiet” and “played favoritism” with several players. Chelsea is among the most high-profile teams in the Premier League and spent £248 million over the offseason on a group of five players: center mid Kai Haverts (£71m), midfielder Hakim Ziyech (£55m), striker Timo Werner (£53m), wingback Ben Chilwell (£45m) and goal keeper Edouard Mendy (£24), meaning their descent appeared evidence as the basis for a change. Photo courtesy of TheSun.co.uk Chelsea fired manager Frank Lampard on Monday with his team sitting in 10th place.

articles.text: As they say nowadays, “Steph gonna Steph.” Warriors superstar Stephen Curry dropped 36 points on the Minnesota Timberwolves on Monday, January 26 in a convincing 130-108 win. After clinging to a dwindling 103-95 lead with 6:45 left in the game, the Warriors rallied for a big victory. That’s when Curry let it rain. A dunk and subsequent taunt by Wolves’ guard Malik Beasley was enough to wake up the Dubs, resulting in Steph scoring 11 points and some ridiculously long 3-pointers, as if that should be any surprise. The Warriors now look ahead to three games they could win, which would set them up nicely prior to a difficult schedule in February. They play their second game against the Timberwolves tonight, the Western Conference’s last-place team. They’ll face seventh place Phoenix Suns tomorrow, and then a game on January 30 against the Detroit Pistons, in last place in the Eastern Conference. But then it gets difficult. On February 2, they’ll play the Celtics, the East’s No. 2 tesm, then the 10th place Mavericks twice (Feb. 4 and 6), followed by backto-back games with the No. 9 Spurs (Feb. 8-9). articles.text: Photo courtesy of Yosemite National Park Service Yosemite National Park will be closed until Saturday, January 30 due to an upcoming storm this week. Yosemite National Park announced on Monday, January 25 that it is closing the entire park until at least Saturday, January 30 due to last week’s Mono windstorm. “Howling winds topple trees, causing power outages and closing Yosemite,” screamed the headlines from Fresno. Winds estimated at 100 mph caused extensive damage in the park, as Yosemite officials anticipated a snowstorm this week. “Park staff continue to clear roads and trails, mitigate hazard trees, and work toward restoring safe conditions for employees and visitors due to last week’s Mono wind event. A significant winter storm is forecast to begin Tuesday night. Hazardous conditions, including substantial snow accumulation, falling trees, and dangerous road conditions, are anticipated through the week,” wrote the park in a statement. Last week’s Mono wind event “clobbered” the park with high winds that knocked over two giant sequoia trees, put thousands of people without power, and caused millions in damages. “They got clobbered this morning,” said National Weather Service representative Andy Bollenbacher yesterday, January 26, “That wasn’t just in Yosemite Valley, but it got down to Wawona as well. We don’t have a lot of observations from that area, but we did record some high winds over 80 mph.” With Yosemite’s re-opening expected to occur on Saturday, weather permitting, patrons will be allowed to have overnight stays in the park after it was limited to day-use visitors in recent months. The park plans to re-open the Upper Pines Campground on February 8, while the historic Yosemite Valley Lodge and The Ahwahnee Hotel will open its doors on February 8. “When the park reopens, it will be open 24 hours per day. Upper Pines Campground will open on February 8. Yosemite Valley Lodge and The Ahwahnee will open on February 5,” wrote the park. With the closure until Saturday, oft used entrances to Bay Area residents like Highway 140’s El Portal Road and Highway 120’s Big Oak Flat Road are currently closed, but will be re-opened after the winter storm. “Visitors will be able to enter the park using El Portal Road (Highway 140), Big Oak Flat Road (Highway 120 from the west), and Hetch Hetchy Road. Areas south of Yosemite Valley (including Badger Pass, Wawona, Mariposa Grove, South Entrance, and Wawona Road) will remain closed until further notice,” wrote park officials. To check current Yosemite Road conditions, visit https:// www.nps.gov/yose/planyourvisit/ conditions.htm, while more lodging information and booking can be found on https://www.nps.gov/ yose/planyourvisit/lodging.htm Here is a direct link to the Upper Pines Campground set to re-open on Feb. 8: https://www. recreation.gov/camping/campgrounds/232447 Photo courtesy of Yosemite National Park Service Several cabins, power lines, and bridges were destroyed in last week’s Mono wind event.
articles.title: Park to re-open with overnight use, limited lodging

articles.text: SF Jazz is celebrating the music of Horace Silver with a special on-demand archival performance of Dee Dee Bridgewater, available to stream now through February 28. The concert was originally performed on September 8, 2017, the opening week of SF Jazz’s season. In this fond remembrance of one of jazz’s greatest composers, Bridgewater pays tribute to Silver with a personal take on his classics. Bridgewater has had a lengthy connection to the composer and pianist beginning in the early 1970s, when her then-husband, trumpeter Cecil Bridgewater, began playing in Silver’s band. She has also featured many of Silver’s classics on her 2005 Grammy-nominated release Love and Peace: A Tribute to Horace Silver. In this performance Bridgewater is joined by trumpeter Theo Croker, saxophonist Irwin Hall, pianist Michael King, bassist SF Jazz presents Dee Dee Bridgewater Eric Wheeler, and drummer Kush Abadey. A special members-only price is offered, but others can rent the performance online as a non-member. For access, click on: https://www.sfjazz. org/sfjazz-digital/rent-dee-deebridgewater/.

articles.text: First concert to premiere February 4 San Francisco Symphony has announced its new season of digital concerts, which will be available on a new video streaming service called “SFSymphony Plus.” New Symphony conductor Esa-Pekka Salonen will program three of the popular “SoundBox” programs, which build on San Francisco Symphony’s series that brought curated music outside of Davies Symphony Hall. Salonen will be joined by some of his collaborative partners, which include soprano Julie Bullock, composer Nico Muhly, flutist Claire Chase, and harpist and singer Destiny Muhammad. The first concert of the season, titled “Nostalgia,” will be on Thursday, February 4, and includes chamber works by Freya Waley-Cohen, Missy Mazzoli, and Caroline Shaw. The new season will bring more episodes in the Symphony’s “Currents” series that began in the sumPhoto by Andrew Eccles San Francisco Symphony Director Esa-Pekka Salonen. mer of 2020. Currents explored musical traditions from around the world that have helped shape the musical culture of the Bay Area. The five-episode series featured the influence of Indian Classical, Native American, Zimbabwean, Persian, and Klezmer music. To obtain tickets for the February 4 concert or any future events, visit https://www.sfsymphonyplus.org/.
articles.title: SF Symphony announces new digital season

articles.text: San Francisco’s Independent Film Festival, which operates under the year-round, non-profit organization SF IndieFest, will begin virtually on Thursday, February 4. articles.text: Fort Mason Drive-In Movie Fort Mason will be hosting Sundance Film Festival satellite screenings, presented by San Francisco’s Roxie Theater. The film follows the life of Ruby, a child of deaf adults who is the only hearing person in her family. When the family’s fishing business is threatened, Ruby finds herself torn between pursuing her love of music and her fear of abandoning her parents. articles.text: Bradley Cooper stars in Limitless. Movie review by Chris Honore’ Likely you’ve seen the commercial: An egg is shown, with voiceover saying, “This is your brain.” The egg is broken and the yoke and white are dropped into a hot frying pan. The voice over then says, “And this is your brain on drugs.” The egg sizzles, the edges grow crispy, even black. It’s a brief, cautionary tale. And so is the intense, very entertaining thriller, Limitless. The film does have a riveting premise. But first, back to the egg. “This is your brain.” And then, “This is your brain on NZT.” No frying pan, just one small, clear tab, placed on the tongue. Within minutes everything glows, bathed in an intense light. All things become possible. If you were cruising through life in first or second gear, using some 20 percent of your brain cells (which, we’re told, is par), with NZT you are suddenly in fourth gear and revving the engine to full capacity. Which is what happens to Eddie Morra (Bradley Cooper) in the story. We first see Eddie – scruffy, depressed, suffering from serious writer’s block – walking down a busy New York City street, wondering where he will find the juice to even write the first sentence of a book for which he has received a generous advance. His long-suffering girlfriend, Lindy (Abbie Cornish), has just broken up with him and he is significantly bummed. That’s when he bumps into his ex-brother-in-law, Vern (Johnny Whitworth), a long-time street hustler and dealer. Vern slips Eddie a small, plastic baggy with a gel-like pill inside and tells him it is FDA approved, no worries. Eddie, at first skeptical, takes it on his way back to his grungy apartment. And that’s when things profoundly change. This pill is not experiential. In other words, it’s not a self-induced hallucination buttressed by a lava lamp. This is extreme fuel injected, pedal to the metal, hyper-cognitive stuff. Eddie writes most of his book in one sitting and looks around and realizes that there are other dragons to slay, like the stock market. It’s at this juncture that things get very tense. Hooked, Eddie returns to Vern’s apartment and tells him that whatever that was, the NZT, well, he’ll need a steady supply. Vern agrees and suggests that first Eddie might go and pick up some breakfast and his dry cleaning. When Eddie returns, things go dark and dicey and Eddie’s path to a brave new world is suddenly replete with predators. Meanwhile, jacked up on NZT, he is transformed: designer clothes, new haircut, and an arbitrage office with computers and graphs, showcasing his newest talents. He’s a rock star of high finance. Limitless is hot. A ride. Flawed to be sure – the ending is a bit weak – but who cares, really? It is simply a good B-movie entertainment. . Limitless. Directed by Neil Burger. Starring Bradley Cooper, Robert DeNiro, Abbie Cornish and Johnny Whitworth. 1 hr., 45 min. Rated PG-13.

articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré It’s important to understand going in that the Harry Potter films – six thus far – are the equivalent of chapters in a book. Each entertains, some more than others, and there is a great deal of backstory already detailed, with more to come. It’s fair to view Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince as a protracted set up for the two-film conclusion (2010 and 2011) of the seven-book saga which has so captured the imaginations of Harry Potterheads worldwide. The books have sold more than 400 million copies and have been translated into 67 languages. Keep in mind that the final Harry Potter novel, Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows, is a 784 page beast weighing 2.4 pounds, a book that small children hauled out of bookstores in their wagons after waiting in long lines, many wearing round peepers. Each of the movies has been solidly entertaining as well as an artful blending of characters, plotting and computer graphics. It must be a thrill for the legions of fans to read and reread the books and then sit in a darkened theater and give themselves over to the sheer wonder of seeing those images they have constructed from the words of J.K. Rowling now on the screen. Half-Blood Prince, coming some eight years since the first film, when Harry (Daniel Radcliffe) was about to turn 11, now shows Harry and Hermione (Emma Watson) and Ron (Rupert Grint) in full-bloom adolescence – hence much of the plot has to do with bumper-car romance and its many inherent misunderstandings. Of course, since Hogwarts is a school of magic, there are love potions being concocted with humorous effects. Lord Voldermot has returned as have the Death Eaters, and there’s a mystery to be solved involving young Voldermot, aka Tom Riddle, Professor Horace Slughorn (Jim Broadbent), Harry, and the head of Hogwarts, Professor Albus Dumbledore (Michael Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince is the sixth installment in the Harry Potter film franchise. Gambon). Without question, the Harry Potter films are filled with some of England’s finest actors, and Half-Blood Prince is no exception. It’s a veritable smorgasbord of fine performances by Gambon (Dumbledore), Broadbent (Slughorn), Robbie Coltrane (Rubeus Hagrid), Maggie Smith (Minerva McGonagall), and, of course, the wonderful Alan Rickman, back again as Severus Snape, a dark, word-clipping character who steals every scene. Can Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince stand alone? No. But it’s not meant to. It is, however, a wonderfully entertaining film that will more than satisfy the millions of Harry Potter fans. In fact, so satisfied are audiences with the series that the first five movies have grossed some $4.8 billion worldwide and counting. As to the question, do you believe in magic?, well, it seems the answer for the countless Potterheads is a loud, unequivocal “Yes!” Harry Potter and the HalfBlood Prince. Directed by David Yates. articles.text: And suddenly, unexpectedly, there she was, Amanda Gorman, 23, wearing a bright yellow blazer, standing behind the podium, America’s National Youth Poet Laureate, waiting to recite her poem, The Hill We Climb, written in the early morning hours of January 7, not long after rioters had stormed the nation’s capitol, their rage still echoing in the now silent corridors, offices and chambers. Her poem – delivered in a strong, clear voice, unencumbered by what had been childhood auditory-speech impediments – was extraordinary, capturing in verse the resilient hope that is embedded in our perpetual quest for a more perfect union. When asked in an interview to comment on her poem, she said, “I’m not going to, in any way, gloss over what we’ve seen over the past few weeks and, dare I say, the past few years. But what I really aspire to do in the poem is to be able to use my words to envision a way in which our country can still come together and can still heal. It’s doing that in a way that is not erasing or neglecting the harsh truths I think America needs to reconcile with.” And with her hands resting on the gunnels of the podium, standing erect, on this singular wintry day, the 20th of January, she began.

articles.text: Editor: The past months have shown us both the fragility and the resilience of our democracy. After a free and fair election, followed by our new president’s inauguration, we find hope and relief in knowing that our institutions have endured. Our democracy marches on, perhaps a bit worse for wear, but we are cleareyed about the challenges and opportunities before us. During the Inauguration, National Youth Poet Laureate and Californian, Amanda Gorman, encapsulated both the pain and the optimism of this moment. In her words: Somehow we’ve weathered and witnessed a nation that isn’t broken but simply unfinished… And yes we are far from polished far from pristine but that doesn’t mean we are striving to form a union that is perfect We are striving to forge a union with purpose To compose a country committed to all cultures, colors, characters and conditions of man As League members, our commitment to empower voters and defend democracy has always driven us to strive for a union that is more perfect. To work with purpose. As we move forward with our next steps working on fair redistricting, policies, and legislation in California, we continue our commitment toward equity-based policies that embrace and lift “all cultures, colors, characters and conditions of man.” The legislative session has kicked off, and we are already working on voting rights legislation and exploring bills related to housing/homelessness, racial justice, criminal justice and policing, climate and environmental justice and so much more. This is our moment. We are “far from polished, far from pristine”, so together, we continue to build a strong, free and just democracy that serves all Californians. Stephanie Doute is Executive Director of the League of Women Voters of California.
articles.title: On American Democracy

articles.text: When day comes we ask ourselves, where can we find light in this never-ending shade? The loss we carry, a sea we must wade. We've braved the belly of the beast, We've learned that quiet isn't always peace, and the norms and notions of what just is isn't always just-ice. And yet the dawn is ours before we knew it. Somehow we do it. Somehow we've weathered and witnessed a nation that isn't broken, but simply unfinished. We the successors of a country and a time where a skinny Black girl descended from slaves and raised by a single mother can dream of becoming president only to find herself reciting for one. And yes we are far from polished. Far from pristine. But that doesn't mean we are striving to form a union that is perfect. We are striving to forge a union with purpose, to compose a country committed to all cultures, colors, characters and conditions of man. And so we lift our gazes not to what stands between us, but what stands before us. We close the divide because we know, to put our future first, we must first put our differences aside. We lay down our arms so we can reach out our arms to one another. We seek harm to none and harmony for all. Let the globe, if nothing else, say this is true, that even as we grieved, we grew, that even as we hurt, we hoped, that even as we tired, we tried, that we'll forever be tied together, victorious. Not because we will never again know defeat, but because we will never again sow division. Scripture tells us to envision that everyone shall sit under their own vine and fig tree and no one shall make them afraid. If we're to live up to our own time, then victory won't lie in the blade. But in all the bridges we've made, that is the promise to glade, the hill we climb. If only we dare. It's because being American is more than a pride we inherit, it's the past we step into and how we repair it. We've seen a force that would shatter our nation rather than share it. Would destroy our country if it meant delaying democracy. And this effort very nearly succeeded. But while democracy can be periodically delayed, it can never be permanently defeated. In this truth, in this faith we trust. For while we have our eyes on the future, history has its eyes on us. This is the era of just redemption we feared at its inception. We did not feel prepared to be the heirs of such a terrifying hour but within it we found the power to author a new chapter. To offer hope and laughter to ourselves. So while once we asked, how could we possibly prevail over catastrophe? Now we assert, How could catastrophe possibly prevail over us? We will not march back to what was, but move to what shall be. A country that is bruised but whole, benevolent but bold, fierce and free. We will not be turned around or interrupted by intimidation, because we know our inaction and inertia will be the inheritance of the next generation. Our blunders become their burdens. But one thing is certain, If we merge mercy with might, and might with right, then love becomes our legacy, and change our children's birthright. So let us leave behind a country better than the one we were left with. Every breath from my bronze-pounded chest, we will raise this wounded world into a wondrous one. We will rise from the gold-limbed hills of the west. We will rise from the windswept northeast, where our forefathers first realized revolution. We will rise from the lake-rimmed cities of the midwestern states. We will rise from the sunbaked south. We will rebuild, reconcile and recover. And every known nook of our nation and every corner called our country, our people diverse and beautiful will emerge, battered and beautiful. When day comes we step out of the shade, aflame and unafraid, the new dawn blooms as we free it. For there is always light, if only we're brave enough to see it. If only we're brave enough to be it.
articles.title: The Hill We Climb

Somehow we do it. Somehow we've weathered and witnessed a nation that isn't broken, but simply unfinished. We the successors of a country and a time where a skinny Black girl descended from slaves and raised by a single mother can dream of becoming president only to find herself reciting for one. And yes we are far from polished. Far from pristine. But that doesn't mean we are striving to form a union that is perfect. We are striving to forge a union with purpose, to compose a country committed to all cultures, colors, characters and conditions of man. And so we lift our gazes not to what stands between us, but what stands before us. We close the divide because we know, to put our future first, we must first put our differences aside. We lay down our arms so we can reach out our arms to one another. We seek harm to none and harmony for all. Let the globe, if nothing else, say this is true, that even as we grieved, we grew, that even as we hurt, we hoped, that even as we tired, we tried, that we'll forever be tied together, victorious. Not because we will never again know defeat, but because we will never again sow division. Scripture tells us to envision that everyone shall sit under their own vine and fig tree and no one shall make them afraid. If we're to live up to our own time, then victory won't lie in the blade. But in all the bridges we've made, that is the promise to glade, the hill we climb. If only we dare. It's because being American is more than a pride we inherit, it's the past we step into and how we repair it. We've seen a force that would shatter our nation rather than share it. articles.text: Dear Jim: I recently had a home inspector give me a list of projects I should focus on. A high priority was my drainage system. Can you tell me why this would be important? And more importantly, how should I approach these issues? Dear Neighbor: While it’s always a bummer to have to pay for work you can’t tangibly see, like a beautiful new kitchen or bath, a homeowner’s value of a properly designed and constructed drainage system is highly underrated. Without proper drainage your house is subject to settlement problems, foundation and slab damage, moisture and mold problems. This is particularly relevant for most of our older homes, where 100-year-old concrete is subject to long-term moisture damage. The cracks you see inside or outside your house may or may not indicate issues with your foundation, but it all starts with drainage. Some common issues are discussed here to help you figure out how drainage may be affecting your home and how to go about fixing it. Unfortunately, drainage is poorly understood. It’s not just about the surface; underground water can be an insidious problem and more difficult and expensive to control. Simply put, you have to deal with water above and below, and they are each approached differently. Surface water is more obvious – water coming from your roof through downspouts and on patios, walkways and driveways needs to be channeled into solid piping and typically brought to the street (or occasionally to your back yard if you have a large lot). Water also flows underground, sometimes very deeply, especially when you are on a hillside with basements or lower levels. This is when and where French drains are needed to control underground water. In order to keep water out of basements or garages with tall foundations, the general concept is to dig the drains below the lowest interior level, which unfortunately can be 8 or 9’ deep with taller fully excavated basement areas. This can be expensive and time-consuming work, requiring the removal of huge amounts of soil and the replacement with similar amounts of gravel backfill. Deeper trenches require procedures to safely dig down deep (shoring) and sometimes material needs to be moved manually by wheelbarrow or buckets through small side-yards, up many stairs, etc. The differences can be night and day between simple downspout projects and deep French drains for highly sloped hillside lots with basements. Costs can vary dramatically. What is supposed to be never was. Most older homes were designed and built without drainage, or with old systems that fail over time. Lacking modern membranes and plastic piping, old clay pipes were used about 50 years ago for French drains, and they were laid in small sections with gaps in between, guaranteeing they were filled with dirt. Many downspouts drain directly on the ground next to the house Proper drainage is cheaper than a new foundation. articles.text: Like a number of concepts in the planning world, open space seems to lack a consistent definition among the various organizations that deal with it. In my experience, simply stated, it most often refers to open land, generally public, without (or with very few) buildings. The universal appreciation of open space is of course due to the many benefits. articles.text: I just sort of stumbled on it. I was vacationing in Mendocino for a week and had done the usual tourist things – the Fern Canyon and Headlands walks, strolling through the town shops and bookstore. I remembered seeing an ad for a winery on the coast about 11 miles north of Mendocino and decided to check it out. It’s hard to describe the experience of rounding the bend on this remote, desolate portion of Hwy 1 and seeing this beautiful, rustic winery perched on the very edge of a cliff overlooking the pounding waves of the Pacific. It is the most stunning setting for a winery I have ever seen – and I have seen a lot of them. The first thing I thought of was “How the heck did this happen? How did this get approved by the California Coastal Commission?” Luckily, we had a chance to meet Sally Ottoson, the owner, who told us the story. Sally is a North Coast native, with roots in Comptche and Ft. Bragg. Because she was a “local”, she was able to talk the property owner into selling to her. Then she set about the long, arduous task of getting approval from the Coastal Commission. Every winery on the coast is required to have a vineyard. So she planted Pinot Noir grapes knowing they would never be any good. It’s far too cold there to grow grapes. The winery imports their grapes from the warmer side of Mendocino county – the Ukiah region on the other side of the coast range. With much perseverance she finally got approval to build the winery. I’m glad she did. We tasted outside socially distanced at a picnic table overlooking the stunning coast. Pacific Star Winery is now open Thursday to Sunday from 12 to 5 p.m., and is closed when it’s raining. Pacific Star Winery sits on the edge of a cliff just south of Westport and north of Fort Bragg. articles.text: Longtime Piedmont resident Frankie Rhodes, a loving wife, mother, grandmother and historic preservationist, passed away peacefully on January 15, 2021 at Alta Bates Hospital in Berkeley surrounded by her loved ones after a long illness. She was known throughout the Bay Area’s historic preservation community, having served more than five decades as a founding member of the Camron-Stanford House Preservation Association (CSHPA). It was charged with the restoration of the last of the 19th-century Victorian mansions that once surrounded Lake Merritt in Oakland. Frankie helped raise more than $800,000 in capital and gifts-in-kind to restore the city-owned building for the community in the early 1970s. The house was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1972 and is cited by the Historic American Building Survey, the California Landmarks Committee and is a City of Oakland landmark. Camron-Stanford House opened to the public in May 1978 and has remained a teaching institution serving Oakland and the greater Bay Area. In addition to her work with Camron-Stanford House, she was active in the Junior League of the East Bay, Decorative Arts Forum, Art League of the East Bay, Oakland Museum docent program, Victorian Alliance and Victorian Society. Born Frances Hayden on August 28, 1939 at UCSF on San Francisco’s Parnassus Hill, she was the daughter of Dr. Charles Thomas Hayden and Margaret Nichols Hayden. She grew up in III and Blake Francis Rhodes. In addition to her work with Camron-Stanford House, she played an instrumental role in beginning a baseball program at her alma mater, the now coed Head-Royce School in Oakland. Both of her sons played on the team during their high school years. For her contributions to the school, she was honored with the Head-Royce School Alumni Association’s Founders Award in 2008. With her mother being born and raised in Hilo, Hawaii, she also was a member of the Daughters of Hawai’i, one of the first organizations in Hawaii to recognize the importance of historic preservation. In a community that prides itself on promoting culture and the arts in our school curriculum, it seems inconceivable that the city council might not renew the Center’s lease. Over the years and with countless numbers of tireless volunteers, the Piedmont Center for the Arts has become a venue for world-class musical events. It has enabled our residents to enjoy outstanding concerts without fighting the traffic and parking in San Francisco and Berkeley. Celebrated musicians from renowned companies have spoken of the venue’s lovely space, its stellar acoustics, and the magnificent Steinway piano. The Center has become a jewel in the crown that is Piedmont, and it saddens me to think of this almost sacred space being used as a community center. Do not let this cultural treasure slip away. As he gazed at the water flowing down Bushy Dell Creek, he realized that perhaps it was merely a mirage. Yes, he decided, it’s not water flowing, it’s all vodka. People have been driven to drink by the pandemic, the drought, the wildfires and the tumult in D.C. on January 6.
